Stage 01

Pre-Incorporation & Know-Your-Customer

UBO transparency, Apostille authentication chain, official name clearance restricted wordlist, and pre-incorporation statutory fee budget.

UBO Ultimate Beneficial Owner Screening Rules Official Registry Only

>=25% ownership / control

Applicable AML statute: Ley 10/2010, de 28 de abril, de prevención del blanqueo de capitales y de la financiación del terrorismo (as amended by Ley 2/2018 and Ley 11/2021); Real Decreto 304/2014, de 5 de mayo (Reglamento SEPBLAC); Real Decreto 1098/2017, de 24 de noviembre (Reglamento del Registro de Titularidades Reales); Real Decreto Legislativo 1/2010, de 2 de julio (Ley de Sociedades de Capital, Articles 9 and 14); EU Directive 2015/849 and EU Directive 2018/843 (transposed); EU AML Regulation 2024/1624 (application phase-in from 2027). UBO definition under Article 4 Ley 10/2010: direct or indirect ownership or control above 25%; where chain analysis cannot identify a natural person above the threshold, senior management is classified as the beneficial owner.
Registered Agent & Physical Address Licensed Agent Required

Acceptable for registration. Article 9 of the Ley de Sociedades de Capital requires the SL to have a registered office in Spain that is effective for legal and administrative service of process. For a remote BPO call center operating without a statutory license, a serviced or virtual office address with genuine mail handling and correspondence capacity satisfies this requirement. The address must correspond to the municipality of the chosen provincial registry, and the notarial deed must identify it. A bare mailbox without administrative substance risks recharacterization by the tax authorities under the 'effective place of management' doctrine, so the virtual office should be supported by a management-services agreement with the serviced-office provider.

✓ Partner licensed company-secretary channels provide local registered address and government mail forwarding.

Stage 02

Statutory Formation & Board Resolutions

Competent registry, governing statute, capital lockup rules, and first board resolution template.

Competent corporate registry

Provincial Mercantile Registry (Registro Mercantil) of the registered office, operating under the Dirección General de Seguridad Jurídica y Fe Pública (Ministry of Justice); corporate name certificates are issued by the Registro Mercantil Central in Madrid.

Governing statute

Real Decreto Legislativo 1/2010, de 2 de julio, por el que se aprueba el texto refundido de la Ley de Sociedades de Capital (LSC), together with the Reglamento del Registro Mercantil (Real Decreto 1784/1996). Key applicable provisions: Art. 4 (minimum share capital), Arts. 19-21 (public deed and registration), Arts. 22-31 (statutory content of the by-laws), Art. 62 (fully paid-up shares), Arts. 124 and 174-175 (appointment of administrators and adoption of first resolutions).

Formation / constitutional filings

Escritura Pública de Constitución (notarial deed of incorporation) followed by inscription in the Registro Mercantil, publication in the BORME (Boletín Oficial del Registro Mercantil), and assignment of the definitive NIF by the Agencia Estatal de Administración Tributaria.

Incorporation processing time

⚡ 53 business days (SOP sum)

Paid-up Capital & Blocked Account Regime No Capital Lockup Account Required

An SL must have share capital of at least €3,000, fully subscribed and fully paid up in cash or in kind before the deed is signed (Art. 62 LSC). The cash capital must be deposited in a Spanish credit institution and the deposit certificate (certificado bancario de desembolso) attached to the deed. A Sociedad Limitada de Formación Sucesiva with capital below €3,000 is permitted under Art. 4.2 LSC, subject to a 20% profit reserve, statutory restrictions on distributions, and limits on corporate debts. Notary and registry arancel fees are payable separately; the former state tax on Operaciones Societarias is not charged for incorporation.

Funding & unlock path: Fire safety certification in accordance with CTE DB-SI (fire resistance, evacuation, detection, and suppression) submitted with the municipal opening licence; structural load inspection by a qualified technician where the building configuration requires it; and work center occupational clearance following compliance with Ley 31/1995 de Prevención de Riesgos Laborales, including risk assessment, designation of a preventive service, and medical surveillance arrangements.

Paid-in capital rule: An SL must have share capital of at least €3,000, fully subscribed and fully paid up in cash or in kind before the deed is signed (Art. 62 LSC). The cash capital must be deposited in a Spanish credit institution and the deposit certificate (certificado bancario de desembolso) attached to the deed. A Sociedad Limitada de Formación Sucesiva with capital below €3,000 is permitted under Art. 4.2 LSC, subject to a 20% profit reserve, statutory restrictions on distributions, and limits on corporate debts. Notary and registry arancel fees are payable separately; the former state tax on Operaciones Societarias is not charged for incorporation.

Pro-Forma First Board Resolution Draft
The Founding Members of [●] S.L., acting as a universal meeting, unanimously resolve that: (1) the company is incorporated under the deed and by-laws, with an object covering multilingual inbound and outbound call center services; (2) the share capital of €3,000, divided into 3,000 participations of €1.00 each, is fully subscribed and paid in cash, evidenced by the blocking deposit certificate of [bank] attached; (3) the registered office is established at [address]; (4) [name] is appointed sole administrator, accepting office; (5) the administrator is empowered to apply for the definitive NIF and complete all commercial, tax and social security registrations.
Industrial Access / EIA & Civil Defense Approval Exempted / Not Required

No industrial installation license applies to a call center/BPO activity under Ley 21/1992 de Industria; reference classification is retained by the Ministerio de Industria, Comercio y Turismo. The activity is subject only to municipal opening control and workplace health and safety compliance.

Category: Municipal 'Licencia de Actividad y Apertura' or 'Declaración Responsable de Apertura' for administrative office premises; no separate industrial or manufacturing permit is required.

Tax ID Application Infrastructure

Competent tax authority

Agencia Estatal de Administración Tributaria (AEAT) - Spanish Tax Agency, official portal https://www.agenciatributaria.es/

E-government filing portal

Spanish SL entities obtain NIF (TIN equivalent) automatically upon incorporation via notary public and Mercantile Registry filing. Foreign-owned SLs follow identical process; non-resident shareholders must appoint a tax representative for AEAT registration and ongoing compliance.

Tax ID type & application path: Entity_Level_Taxation — Spanish SL entities obtain NIF (TIN equivalent) automatically upon incorporation via notary public and Mercantile Registry filing. Foreign-owned SLs follow identical process; non-resident shareholders must appoint a tax representative for AEAT registration and ongoing compliance.

Default Tax Classification & Elections

Default tax classification

Entity_Level_Taxation

Available election forms

No check-the-box elections; Spanish SLs are subject to mandatory entity-level taxation under Impuesto sobre Sociedades. Limited statutory regimes available for holding companies or hybrid mismatches, but no broad elective treatment for non-residents.

VAT / GST & 0% Export Zero-Rating

Standard VAT / GST rate

21%

Mandatory registration threshold (Nexus)

300,000 EUR

Export 0% zero-rating conditions

0% VAT applies to exports of goods outside the EU or offshore services supplied to non-EU clients, provided strict documentary proof of export and non-resident recipient status.

  • Customs Export Declaration, Bill of Lading, Inward Remittance Certificate

Mandatory real-time facturación electrónica for all taxable supplies; full API integration with AEAT required for issuance of digital stamps, invoice validation, and clearance compliance.

AEAT may conduct retrospective audits resulting in penalties up to 100% of evaded tax plus interest and surcharges; fraudulent zero-rating claims trigger criminal prosecution and full clawback of benefits.

Stage 04

Banking & Treasury Architecture

Central-bank FX diagnosis, tier-1 local banks vs offshore digital EMI matrix, and KYC rejection defense guide.

Foreign Exchange Regime & Central Bank Policy

Current-account convertibility

Spain uses the euro, which is fully convertible for ordinary current-account and capital-account transactions. Spain has no general exchange-control regime, no general requirement to obtain prior approval for foreign investment funding, and no general restriction on repatriation of dividends, interest, service fees, liquidation proceeds, or intercompany balances. Payments remain subject to bank AML, sanctions, beneficial-ownership, tax-residency, transfer-pricing, and source-of-funds controls. Dividend distributions require distributable profits, satisfaction of Spanish corporate-law reserve requirements, approval of annual accounts and the distribution, and applicable withholding-tax analysis. Outbound payments to related parties or low-tax jurisdictions may receive enhanced scrutiny and must be supported by contracts, evidence of services, arm's-length pricing, and tax documentation. Cross-border payments may also trigger statistical reporting, foreign-investment reporting, or information requests depending on transaction type, counterparty, amount, and reporting thresholds.

Export proceeds surrender rules

Spain has no statutory general obligation requiring a Spanish Sociedad de Responsabilidad Limitada to repatriate export proceeds to Spain, surrender foreign-currency receipts, convert receipts into euros, or convert a prescribed percentage within a fixed period. The company may retain foreign-currency balances with an authorized institution, subject to its bank's account terms and applicable reporting obligations. For a BPO and call-center business, receipts are generally service-export receipts rather than merchandise-export proceeds. The company should maintain invoices, contracts, service-delivery evidence, VAT treatment, customer due-diligence records, bank advices, and reconciliation between invoicing, collections, and accounting. Any applicable Banco de España external-sector or foreign-investment reporting must be assessed by transaction type and threshold; such reporting is not a currency-surrender requirement.

Central bank supervision: Banco de España, operating within the Eurosystem under the monetary authority of the European Central Bank; foreign-exchange and payment-services rules are principally derived from European Union law, Spanish banking law, anti-money-laundering legislation, and Banco de España supervisory requirements.

Offshore Digital Bank / EMI Whitelist

Wise Fit: High

Medium to High for supplementary collections, payments, and foreign-currency treasury; Low to Medium as the sole banking relationship. Wise Europe SA and comparable providers may offer business payment services to eligible Spanish companies, but availability depends on product scope, residence, industry, transaction profile, currencies, and risk approval. An electronic-money institution is not generally a deposit-taking bank, and safeguarded customer funds do not provide the same deposit-protection or credit facilities as bank deposits. The company should retain a Spanish or other EEA bank as its primary account for share-capital evidence, payroll, taxes, regulated counterparties, liquidity reserves, and contingency access. EMI accounts may be restricted for client-money flows, nested payment activity, high-volume consumer payments, cash-like transactions, sanctioned geographies, virtual-asset activity, or unexplained third-party receipts. Use of Wise B2B or another EMI must comply with its user agreement, PSD2-related requirements, Spanish AML rules, sanctions controls, and complete source-of-funds documentation.

Core KYC Rejection Triggers & Defense Dossier

Foreign shareholder or director with incomplete identification, expired passport, inconsistent spelling, or undocumented tax residence.

Root cause: Foreign shareholder or director with incomplete identification, expired passport, inconsistent spelling, or undocumented tax residence.

Defense evidence: Current passport or national identity document; proof of residential address; foreign tax-identification evidence; certified Spanish or English translation where requested; notarized, apostilled, or legalized documents where required; completed tax-residency self-certification; and a signed ownership and control chart.
Unclear ultimate beneficial ownership or nominee, trust, holding-company, or multi-layer corporate ownership.

Root cause: Unclear ultimate beneficial ownership or nominee, trust, holding-company, or multi-layer corporate ownership.

Defense evidence: Group structure chart to natural-person ultimate owners; certificates of incorporation and good standing for each relevant entity; shareholder registers; constitutional documents; director registers; trust or foundation instruments where applicable; beneficial-owner declarations; corporate resolutions; and evidence of control rights.
New SL with no operating history and projected cross-border receipts that appear disproportionate to paid-in capital.

Root cause: New SL with no operating history and projected cross-border receipts that appear disproportionate to paid-in capital.

Defense evidence: Detailed business plan; signed or draft customer contracts; pricing schedule; sales pipeline; staffing plan; expected monthly transaction matrix by country, currency, payer, and purpose; 12-month cash-flow forecast; source-of-funds evidence for shareholders; and explanation of why operating receipts exceed initial capital.
BPO activity involving high-volume outbound tele-sales, consumer data, commission flows, or payments received for third parties.

Root cause: BPO activity involving high-volume outbound tele-sales, consumer data, commission flows, or payments received for third parties.

Defense evidence: Service agreements; evidence that the company is a service provider rather than a payment intermediary; customer and payer-flow diagram; prohibition of unauthorized client-money commingling; data-protection and call-compliance policies; sample invoices; merchant or platform agreements; and written confirmation of who bears refund, chargeback, and consumer-law obligations.
Payments involving Latin America, high-risk jurisdictions, sanctioned countries, politically exposed persons, or counterparties with opaque ownership.

Root cause: Payments involving Latin America, high-risk jurisdictions, sanctioned countries, politically exposed persons, or counterparties with opaque ownership.

Defense evidence: Country-risk policy; sanctions-screening procedure; payer and beneficiary identification; beneficial-owner checks; adverse-media results; transaction rationale; contracts and invoices; proof of services; escalation records; and documented refusal procedures for prohibited or unexplained transactions.
Frequent inbound payments from unrelated third parties or receipts that do not match customer invoices.

Root cause: Frequent inbound payments from unrelated third parties or receipts that do not match customer invoices.

Defense evidence: Aged accounts-receivable ledger; invoice-to-bank reconciliation; customer master file; contractual assignment or agency documentation; payment remittance information; explanation of marketplace or group-company settlement arrangements; and controls preventing pass-through payment activity.
Use of personal accounts, virtual offices, unverified remote workers, or an address inconsistent with the declared business.

Root cause: Use of personal accounts, virtual offices, unverified remote workers, or an address inconsistent with the declared business.

Defense evidence: Commercial lease or registered-office evidence; utility or occupancy documentation; payroll or contractor records; employment and outsourcing agreements; operational workflow; technology and telephony records; and a written segregation policy prohibiting personal-account use.
Tax-compliance or CRS/FATCA information mismatch, including missing Spanish tax identification number or inconsistent entity classification.

Root cause: Tax-compliance or CRS/FATCA information mismatch, including missing Spanish tax identification number or inconsistent entity classification.

Defense evidence: Spanish tax identification certificate; deed and commercial-registry extract; corporate-tax registration evidence; CRS self-certification; FATCA classification where relevant; VAT registration or non-registration explanation; accounting contact details; and confirmation of tax-residence country.
Expected use of cash, prepaid instruments, cryptocurrency, or unregulated payment providers.

Root cause: Expected use of cash, prepaid instruments, cryptocurrency, or unregulated payment providers.

Defense evidence: Treasury policy showing bank-only settlement; documented prohibition of cash and crypto exposure unless separately approved; approved-provider list; transaction-monitoring controls; and independent evidence that all proposed payment providers are licensed or appropriately supervised.

Cross-Border Clearing Corridors & Settlement Fit

Route shareholder funding from an account held in the shareholder's legal name to the SL's account with an EEA bank using SEPA Credit Transfer for euro funding or SWIFT for non-SEPA currencies. Before remittance, complete the corporate resolution, subscription or loan agreement, source-of-funds file, beneficial-owner review, and accounting classification. Use an unambiguous payment narrative such as 'share capital contribution', 'shareholder loan', or 'capital increase funding', and do not describe debt as equity or equity as revenue. For a capital increase, coordinate the bank certificate or other evidence required by the Spanish notary and Commercial Registry, and retain proof of receipt and subsequent registration. For shareholder loans, retain executed loan terms, maturity, interest, repayment mechanics, transfer-pricing support, and withholding-tax analysis. The bank may request purpose information, LEI or corporate identifiers, payer ownership evidence, and supporting agreements. There is no general Spanish FX authorization or mandatory conversion into euros. Reconcile every transfer to the general ledger and report any applicable foreign-investment or external-sector information through the prescribed channel when the relevant threshold or transaction category is met.For ordinary BPO service payments, use SEPA Credit Transfer or SEPA Instant where available for euro payments and SWIFT customer credit transfers for non-SEPA currencies. A SWIFT MT103 is the traditional customer-payment message; banks may now process the equivalent payment through ISO 20022 payment messages. Include complete ordering-customer, beneficiary, account, address, invoice, and purpose information. For supplier or cross-border service settlements, retain contract, invoice, proof of performance, VAT and withholding-tax analysis, and sanctions-screening evidence. Commercial letters of credit are generally unnecessary for ordinary BPO services but may be used for qualifying cross-border purchases or structured trade transactions through a bank, subject to documentary-compliance rules, UCP 600 where incorporated, sanctions review, and bank credit approval. For recurring payroll, tax, and supplier liquidity, use controlled payment batches with dual approval, beneficiary validation, positive pay or equivalent controls, and daily bank reconciliation. Avoid third-party settlement unless contractually documented and approved by the bank.Deliverable EUR/USD and other currency forwards entered with an authorized bank or appropriately regulated investment firm, supported by documented underlying exposures, treasury limits, counterparty limits, confirmation procedures, and accounting treatment.Non-deliverable forwards may be available for restricted or non-convertible currencies and are generally cash-settled in an agreed reference currency; availability is bank-dependent and subject to MiFID II conduct, appropriateness or professional-client classification, EMIR reporting and risk-mitigation requirements where applicable, sanctions controls, and documented commercial exposure.Currency swaps and cross-currency interest-rate swaps may be used for funding or longer-term liquidity management with an authorized counterparty, subject to ISDA or equivalent documentation, collateral terms, valuation, close-out, EMIR requirements, board approval, and counterparty-credit limits.FX spot transactions and scheduled conversions may be used for ordinary operating needs; treasury should avoid speculative positions, maintain an exposure register, and match hedge tenor, notional amount, and currency to forecast receipts or payments.Options and collars may be available from regulated counterparties but require separate suitability, premium, valuation, accounting, and governance analysis; they should not be used without written treasury-policy authorization and clear evidence of the underlying exposure.

E-commerce / gateway settlement fit: Medium to High for supplementary collections, payments, and foreign-currency treasury; Low to Medium as the sole banking relationship. Wise Europe SA and comparable providers may offer business payment services to eligible Spanish companies, but availability depends on product scope, residence, industry, transaction profile, currencies, and risk approval. An electronic-money institution is not generally a deposit-taking bank, and safeguarded customer funds do not provide the same deposit-protection or credit facilities as bank deposits. The company should retain a Spanish or other EEA bank as its primary account for share-capital evidence, payroll, taxes, regulated counterparties, liquidity reserves, and contingency access. EMI accounts may be restricted for client-money flows, nested payment activity, high-volume consumer payments, cash-like transactions, sanctioned geographies, virtual-asset activity, or unexplained third-party receipts. Use of Wise B2B or another EMI must comply with its user agreement, PSD2-related requirements, Spanish AML rules, sanctions controls, and complete source-of-funds documentation.

Stage 06

Corporate Tax & Transfer Pricing

Corporate income tax (CIT), box-by-box return breakdown, dividend WHT, and director personal liability.

Statutory corporate income tax (CIT)

25%

Dividend withholding tax (WHT)

19% on dividends paid to non-resident shareholders without a permanent establishment; 24% applies to residents of non-EU/EEA or treaty-less jurisdictions. The rate is reduced to 0% for qualifying EU parent companies holding at least 5% of the Spanish SL for 12 months under the EU Parent-Subsidiary Directive.

Mandatory Return Breakdown

Deadline: · Frequency:

Within 6 months and 25 days after the end of the tax period; for a 31 December fiscal year-end, the due date is 25 July of the following year.

Box-by-Box Return Breakdown (non-resident focus)

BoxField Non-resident guidanceTax-evasion pitfall
Line 1 (Identificación del contribuyente) NIF (tax ID), registered legal name, NACE/ISIC code 7820, registered address and the residency country of any non-resident beneficial owners. The SL remains the Spanish tax resident; non-resident shareholders must not be shown as issuer of the Spanish entity's invoices. Any foreign branch or permanent establishment derived from remote BPO activities must be separately reported to avoid PE exposure. Late filing without prior AEAT request incurs a surcharge under Article 27 LGT of 5% plus 1% per full month of delay, capped at 20% of the self-assessed liability. If AEAT requires the filing, penalties escalate to 50%-150% under Article 191 LGT, plus late-payment interest. Zero-liability returns attract fixed penalties of EUR 100, or EUR 200 where gross receipts exceed EUR 5,000,000, with an additional EUR 5 per omitted data element. Failure to file quarterly instalments (Modelo 202) adds separate surcharges under Article 26 LGT.
Line 2 (Resultado contable del ejercicio) Accounting profit or loss before income tax from the financial statements prepared under Spanish GAAP (PGC), reflecting all retiro BPO and call-centre service revenues and costs. Intercompany transactions with offshore related call-centre entities must be recorded and eliminated or adjusted at arm's length; no margin of the Spanish SL may be shifted without a valid transfer-pricing study. Line 3 (Ajustes extracontables – permanentes y temporales) Schedule of permanent reconciliations (non-deductible penalties, representation expenses above statutory limits) and temporary differences (accelerated depreciation, provisions). Management fees or royalties paid to foreign related companies must be supported by contracts, actual service evidence and arm's-length pricing; any expenditure lacking economic substance will be recharacterized and adjusted. Foreign shareholders cannot transfer tax losses unless a formally approved Spanish merger or tax-group provision applies; documentation must trace each carryforward to the originating Spanish taxpayer. Line 5 (Base imponible y tipo de gravamen) Taxable base after loss offset, to which the 25% standard rate (or 15% new-entity rate) is applied. Since the SL is a resident entity, its worldwide income is taxed in Spain. Withholding on the SL's future dividend distributions is separate and reported via Modelo 216/296; it must not be presented as a tax credit of the SL in Form 200. Transfer Pricing & Economic Substance

Master / Local File threshold: EUR 45,000,000 net turnover threshold for full Master File and Local File documentation under Art. 13 RD 634/2015; smaller resident SLs must prepare simplified documentation when related-party transactions exceed EUR 100,000 per related counterparty or EUR 250,000 in aggregate during the tax period, and must still file Form 232 for related-party transactions.

Economic substance scope: Spain does not apply the offshore Economic Substance Regulations (ESR) found in common-law financial centres; however, AEAT invokes the abuse-of-law doctrine (Art. 15 LGT) and substance-over-form principles to disregard Spanish SLs lacking real premises, local management, employees and commercial decision-making power, especially where the remote BPO structure is purely a conduit. A Spanish SL carrying out call-centre functions must evidence local supervisory staff, telephony or IT contracts, client agreements executed in Spain and actual operational control to secure treaty eligibility and avoid permanent establishment attribution.

Fatal Compliance Red Lines & Director Liability

Tax Evasion – Corporate Income Tax Fraud (Art. 305 Código Penal)

Statutory sanction: Imprisonment of 2 to 6 years, fines of 2-6 times the defrauded tax, loss of subsidies and public procurement rights, and administrative penalties of 50% to 150% of the tax deficiency under Article 191 LGT.

Director personal liability: Directors are jointly and severally liable for the defrauded corporate tax debt. In criminal tax fraud they face travel bans, disqualification from acting as administrators for up to 10 years, personal asset attachment and imprisonment where a shell structure was used to conceal ownership or revenues.
Transfer Pricing and Documentation Breach (Art. 18 LIS, Art. 191 LGT)

Statutory sanction: AEAT may assess additional taxable income; incomplete transfer-pricing documentation triggers a penalty of 15% of the value of the related-party operations, while the total absence of documentation leads to a 50% penalty on the tax-base adjustment, plus late-payment interest and surcharges.

Director personal liability: Directors who sign fictitious intercompany agreements or authorize non-compliant transfer-pricing policies may be held personally liable for the unpaid tax debt. Deliberate manipulation of intercompany margins can also ground criminal prosecution, travel restrictions and disqualification orders.
Employment and Social Security Evasion (Art. 307 Código Penal)

Statutory sanction: Recovery of unpaid social security contributions plus surcharges of at least 20%, administrative sanctions up to EUR 187,515 for very serious violations; criminal liability with imprisonment of 3 to 6 months and fines if the defrauded social security amount exceeds EUR 50,000.

Director personal liability: Directors are criminally responsible for unpaid social security amounts and may face corporate veil piercing, forced contribution from personal assets, travel bans and disqualification from public benefits. Persistent unlawful conduct can trigger a judicial prohibition from managing companies for several years.
Shell Company / Economic Substance Failure / AML Deficiency

Statutory sanction: The SL may be taxed as a disregarded entity with attribution of Spanish-source income to the foreign principal, and the foreign shareholder may become exposed to a Spanish permanent establishment. Violations of AML Law 10/2010 carry fines up to EUR 5,000,000; financial authorities may freeze accounts, issue cease-and-desist orders and revoke payment-rail access.

Director personal liability: Directors face judicial lifting of the corporate veil, effectively removing limited liability, with attachment of personal assets, travel bans, and potential imprisonment for money laundering if funds are knowingly routed through a purely artificial Spanish entity.
